paragraphs.text: Those copper dots on jeans started on horse blankets.

Start with the detail itself. Those copper dots on jeans started on horse blankets. A tailor borrowed them for work trousers. In Reno, tailor Jacob Davis used rivets on pocket corners that tore apart. He couldn't afford a patent, so he asked Levi Strauss to apply with him. In 1873 they patented an improvement in fastening pocket openings. But back-pocket rivets scratched furniture and saddles. From 1937 they were covered, and by 1966 they were gone. The rivets you see now still guard the most vulnerable spots.

Its history begins with a practical problem. Jacob Davis pioneered rivets on work trousers in 1871 while working as a tailor in Reno, Nevada. Davis had originally used rivets on horse blankets. In 1873 the pair received a patent for an improvement in fastening pocket openings.
That problem shaped the design. Rivets reinforced stress points such as back-pocket corners and the crotch, which often tore apart under heavy wear.

The documentation makes the purpose clearer. The governing physics: Rivets reinforce stress points such as pocket corners that tore apart under heavy wear. Davis did not have the money to patent the technique, so he asked Levi Strauss to apply with him. Copper rivets kept pockets from ripping and made the openings stronger.

But one detail complicates the familiar story. The rivets look decorative, but they began as reinforcement borrowed from horse blankets. In 1937 Levi's began covering back-pocket rivets because the copper points scratched furniture and saddles.

The design did not stop changing there. Riveted work trousers became the blue jean; back-pocket rivets were later covered and then removed. The covered back-pocket rivets were dropped altogether by 1966 because they wore through the denim.
Now the opening question has a precise answer. Rivets continue to strengthen the most vulnerable parts of jeans.
